paragraphs.heading: Earth's thin outer skin
paragraphs.text: Earth's crust is the planet's outer shell of rock, making up less than one percent of its radius and volume. It is the top part of the lithosphere, the solid outer division of Earth that includes the crust and the upper mantle. The crust sits on the mantle, an arrangement that stays stable because the upper mantle's rock, peridotite, is much denser. The base of the crust is usually placed at the Mohorovičić discontinuity, a boundary where the speed of seismic waves changes.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of crust
paragraphs.text: Continental crust is 25 to 70 km thick and made mostly of lighter rocks such as granite. Under a few places, like the Tibetan Plateau and the Altiplano, it reaches 50 to 80 km. Oceanic crust is only 5 to 10 km thick and made mainly of denser rocks such as basalt, diabase and gabbro. On average the crust is about 15 to 20 km thick.

paragraphs.heading: Floating on the mantle
paragraphs.text: Both kinds of crust are less dense than the mantle beneath, so both float on it. Continental crust is thicker and lighter, so it rides higher, an example of isostasy. That is why continents stand as high ground with deep ocean basins around them. The lithosphere is also broken into tectonic plates, and their motion lets heat escape from Earth's interior into space.

paragraphs.heading: Hotter and heavier with depth
paragraphs.text: The crust warms as you go down, locally by as much as 30 °C per kilometer near the top. At its boundary with the mantle it typically reaches about 700 to 1,600 °C. In continental crust feldspars are the commonest minerals, about 41% of the mass; quartz makes up 12% and pyroxenes 11%. Its density rises from about 2.66 g/cm³ near the top to 3.1 g/cm³ at the base.

paragraphs.heading: The first crust is gone
paragraphs.text: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago, and the heat of its growth melted it completely. As that growth slowed, Earth cooled and formed its first crust, called primary crust. Large impacts probably destroyed it again and again, and it reformed each time from the leftover magma ocean. None of it survives today; erosion, impacts and plate tectonics wiped it all away.

paragraphs.heading: Young oceans, old continents
paragraphs.text: Since then Earth has made a secondary crust, the oceanic kind, and a tertiary crust, the continental kind. Ocean crust forms at mid-ocean spreading centers, where partly melted mantle gives basaltic magma. Old ocean crust is destroyed at subduction zones, trenches where an ocean plate sinks back into the mantle. So the oldest ocean crust today is only about 200 million years old. Most continental crust is far older: its oldest rocks are about 3.7 to 4.28 billion years old, found in places such as Western Australia and Canada's Northwest Territories.
